query: For a high-entropy alloy initially designed as a single-phase solid solution, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why it loses toughness or undergoes brittle fracture under mechanical loading in demanding engineering service? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, identify the applicable service and loading boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: During mechanical loading, the homogeneous single-phase HEA experiences stress‐assisted atomic rearrangements that promote the nucleation of fine, brittle secondary phases (e.g., intermetallic or ordered clusters) preferentially at grain boundaries, thereby reducing toughness and leading to brittle fracture under demanding service loads.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase solid solution high-entropy alloy with a uniform microstructure (e.g., FCC or BCC) as originally designed.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled mechanical loading (monotonic tensile and creep tests) at service-relevant temperatures using samples prepared in the as-cast, homogeneous state.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted at room temperature up to moderate elevated temperatures under tensile and creep loading conditions that simulate demanding engineering service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and localized accumulation of fine, brittle precipitates or ordered clusters—most notably along grain boundaries—induced by stress-driven atomic diffusion and dislocation activity.
generation.mechanism: Under mechanical loading, enhanced dislocation motion and stress-assisted diffusion cause local compositional fluctuations and atomic rearrangements. These changes drive a transformation from the initial single-phase state to a microstructure with brittle secondary phases that act as crack initiation sites, thereby compromising toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline homogeneous HEA, mechanically loaded samples will exhibit microstructural evidence (via TEM/XRD) of new secondary phases or ordering at grain boundaries. Concurrently, fracture testing will reveal a reduction in toughness and a shift from ductile failure to brittle fracture behaviors.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, single-phase HEA that shows consistently high toughness and ductility when unloaded or subjected to milder conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under service conditions involving tensile or creep loading at room temperature and modestly elevated temperatures. It may not hold if the loading mode or temperature regime falls outside of the range where stress-assisted diffusion is significant.
generation.uncertainty: The exact identity, volume fraction, and kinetics of the stress-induced secondary phases may vary with composition and testing conditions; further investigation is needed to quantify these effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical single-phase HEA samples. One set is subjected to controlled tensile and creep tests under service-relevant conditions, while the other set serves as the untreated baseline. Employ in-situ or post-mortem microscopy (TEM, SEM) and XRD analysis to identify any formation of secondary brittle phases or ordering transitions, and perform fracture toughness tests (e.g., by measuring ductility and crack propagation behavior).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If mechanically loaded samples show no evidence of the predicted secondary phase formation or ordering transition (i.e., maintain a homogeneous single-phase microstructure) and retain toughness and ductile fracture behavior comparable to the baseline samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

This paper examines the microstructure and mechanical properties of Ta 20 Nb 20 Hf 20 Zr 20 Ti 20 . Two casting processes, namely, gravity casting and suction-assisted casting, were applied, both followed by Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP). The aim of the current study was to investigate the creep and tensile properties of the material, since the literature review revealed no data whatsoever regarding these properties. The main findings are that the HIP process is responsible for the appearance of a Hexagonal Close Packed (HCP) phase that is dispersed differently in these two castings. The HIP process also led to a considerable increase in the mechanical properties of both materials under compression, with values found to be higher than those reported in the literature. Contrary to the compression properties, both materials were found to be highly brittle under tension, either during room temperature tension tests or creep tests conducted at 282 °C. Fractography yielded brittle fracture without any evidence of plastic deformation prior to fracture.

The tensile creep behavior of an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy was systematically investigated over an intermediate temperature range (500–600 °C) and applied stress (140–400 MPa). The alloy exhibited a stress-dependent transition from a low-stress region (LSR-region I) to a high-stress region (HSR-region II). The LSR was characterized by a stress exponent of 5 to 6 and an average activation energy of 268 kJ mol −1 , whereas the HSR showed much higher corresponding values of 8.9–14 and 380 kJ mol −1 . Microstructural examinations on the deformed samples revealed remarkable dynamic recrystallization at higher stress levels. Dislocation jogging and tangling configurations were frequently observed in LSR and HSR at 550 and 600 °C, respectively. Moreover, dynamic precipitates identified as M 23 C 6 or a Cr-rich σ phase were formed along grain boundaries in HSR. The diffusion-compensated strain rate versus modulus-compensated stress data analysis implied that the creep deformation in both stress regions was dominated by stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion.
